newsitem.title: UK: Dlr crawls up in Europe after overnight drubbing.
newsitem.headline: Dlr crawls up in Europe after overnight drubbing.

text.p: The dollar struggled in morning Europe after being beaten down by more than two yen in overnight trade, but analysts said a further plunge was unlikely even though the U.S. currency still looked sickly.
Top-level Japanese officials jumped in to try and stem the dollar's freefall, saying the Group of Seven agreement reached in April had filtered through to the markets "sufficiently".

Such comments -- made by Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka and Eisuke Sakakibara, head of the finance ministry's international finance bureau -- had their effect, pulling the dollar off 115.60 yen, its lowest level since January 10.
Dollar/yen was at 116.10/20 at 0750 GMT, still almost two yen below its Wednesday late European level of 117.95/05.
Analysts said the dollar would likely settle down for now, mainly because dollar/yen now seemed to be in an area which would keep both the U.S. and Japan satisfied.
Also, dollar/yen's latest slide has been unsustainably rapid, they said. The overnight drop means the dollar has slid 12 yen since it hit a 55-month high of 127.47 on May 1.
"I can see it heading towards 115 yen, but there should be consolidation throughout the week around 115-120, with a very modest upside bias," said Stephen Hannah at IBJ International.
"They (the Japanese) didn't want the yen to be a one-way sell, and now it appears there's a two-way rather than one-way risk," said Hannah, who is director of research at IBJ.

Behind the dollar's tumble overnight was market speculation that the U.S. would support a stronger yen. Such speculation started in New York trade, fuelled by talk that a newsletter from a Washington-based consulting firm stated Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin was calling for a dollar/yen rate of 115.
Subscribers to the newsletter contacted by Reuters denied receiving such a report.
Analysts said this was leading to a market consensus that a level of around 115 yen or slightly below was likely to keep the authorities fairly happy on both sides of the Pacific.
"The Japanese, for their part, don't want a really strong yen because of their export industry," said Adrian Davies, senior strategist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull here.
"So basically there is a comfort zone that both the U.S. and Japan would be happy with, and when the dollar gets down to around 115 yen, the Japanese will say 'no more'," Davies said.
Meanwhile, the market was keenly awaiting a slew of U.S. data due today for further clues on U.S. interest rates.

April consumer prices at 1230 GMT would be the highlight, as a bigger-than-expected drop in producer prices on Wednesday shocked the market and further clouded prospects of a rate hike at the policy-making Federal Open Market Committee meeting on May 20. CPI is forecast to rise 0.1 percent on the month and 2.6 percent on the year against rises of 0.1 and 2.8 previously.
Analysts said the market would be wary of driving the dollar down further ahead of today's data.
"There is still need for caution. The market's priced as if the Fed won't raise rates but even if the data is benign, there is still a chance of a rate hike," IBJ's Hannah said.

SocGen's Davies said today's data would likely put the US-Japan yield differential in the minds of market operators again. The wide yield gap had been a major engine behind dollar/yen's rally to a 55-month high earlier this month.

Noting that Japan's April department store sales data announced overnight were much weaker than expected, he added that although this was largely due to a sales tax hike on April 1 and not a permanent trend, it still did not bode well.
"There were only mild signs of Japanese economic recovery anyway, so it has set back the timing for a Japanese rate hike," Davies said. -- Chizu Nomiyama, London Forex, +44-171-542-6721
